newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu eyes trade ties in Moscow trip.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu eyes trade ties in Moscow trip.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu arrived in Moscow on Monday on his first trip to Russia since becoming prime minister nine months ago and said he hoped to boost economic ties between the two countries.
Russia, keen to revive its influence in Middle East peace talks, will host Netanyahu for 48 hours after a similar trip by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat last month.

"Israel is prepared to cooperate with Russia economically. We have a great future together," Netanyahu told reporters at the elegant Metropol hotel where he had been invited to dinner by Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov.

"Israel is fast becoming the Silicon Valley of the eastern hemisphere. We have more scientists per capita than any other country," he said, adding that many of these scientists were of Russian origin and could be a bridge to greater cooperation.
But Netanyahu made no comment on the deepening crisis at home where his troop redeployment plan sparked angry clashes on Monday between Israeli soldiers and Palestinians.

His foreign policy adviser Dore Gold told Reuters that Netanyahu would raise the issue of sales of advanced military technology to Iran and Syria, the Jewish state's arch-foes, during his Moscow talks.

Last month the Los Angeles Times said U.S. intelligence reports indicated Russia had given Iran technology for the Russian SS-4 missile, which has a range almost three times greater than that of any missile now in Tehran's arsenal. Moscow denied the report.
Netanyahu said last week he would press Russia not to help Iran develop ballistic missiles.
Reinforcing Israel's concerns, its ambassador to Moscow Aliza Shenar told Ekho Moskvy radio on Monday that Russian cooperation with Iran in the nuclear field was a major worry.
"Israel is unhappy with the fact that Russia is selling weapons to Iran and cooperating with it in the area of nuclear energy," said Shenar.
Netanyahu, whose country wants to diversify its energy sources, is expected to discuss the purchase of natural gas from Russia during his trip.
Shenar said the construction of a gas pipeline through Turkey was one of the projects on the agenda. The two countries will sign a customs agreement during the visit, she added.
Netanyahu, 47, also plans to meet Russian businessmen and the Moscow Jewish community before completing his trip in Russia's second city, St Petersburg.

More than 650,000 Jews have moved to Israel from the former Soviet Union since Moscow flung open the doors to emigration in 1989 in an era of glasnost or openness, and Netanyahu's government includes several prominent former Russians, including former Soviet Jewish dissident Natan Sharansky.
Moscow re-established long-severed ties with Israel only in 1991 for the launch of Arab-Israeli peace talks in Madrid co-sponsored by the United States and the then-Soviet Union.

"It is very good that the Russian leadership meets today with all sides, both with the Israelis and the Arabs. This can only facilitate dialogue and the lowering of tensions in the region," ambassador Shenar said in her radio interview.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, an Arabic speaker with long experience of the Middle East, wants to boost Moscow's regional clout, much weakened by its economic woes. In Soviet times Moscow was a strong supporter of Palestinian self-rule, helping to balance Washington's pro-Israel stance.

The late Yitzhak Rabin made the first visit of an Israeli prime minister to Moscow in 1994. Sharansky, now trade minister, returned in January on his first trip since being freed from a KGB jail and turned over to the West in a 1986 prisoner swap.
